

    DETAILED ACTION
Response to Amendment
Applicant’s amendment filed 30 July 2009 amends claims 1, 3, 5, 11, 18, 22, 24, and 27. Claim 2 has been cancelled. Claims 28-34 have been added. Applicant’s amendment has been fully considered and entered.
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s argument that “Mathers…does not disclose or suggest…updatable by a provider of the digital object using a secure channel after distribution of the secure hardware adjunct to the end user," has been fully considered and are persuasive.  Therefore, the rejection has been withdrawn.  However, upon further consideration, a new ground(s) of rejection is made in view of Qawami, U.S. Publication No. 2007/0056042.
Applicant’s arguments, with respect to the §112 rejections has been fully considered and are persuasive.  The previous §112 rejections have been withdrawn. 
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(e) the invention was described in (1) an application for patent, published under section 122(b), by another filed in the United States before the invention by the applicant for patent or (2) a patent granted on an application for patent by another filed in the United States before the invention by the applicant for patent, except that an international application filed under the treaty defined in section 351(a) shall have the effects for purposes of this subsection of an application filed in the United States only if the international application designated the United States and was published under Article 21(2) of such treaty in the English language.

Claims 27, 30, 31, 34 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by Qawami, U.S. Publication No. 2007/0056042. Referring to claims 27, 30, 31, 34, Qawami discloses providing at least a portion of a digital object on a first part of a hardware element that is visible to a user (Figure 2), providing user-access control on a second party of the hardware element that is invisible to the user ([0093]). Qawami discloses a content distribution system wherein content is distributed to end users via smart cards ([0006]-[0007]). The content is stored along with a rights object that governs how/when the content can be accessed ([0009]). The rights can dictate that the content can be accessed for a limited time, and the user is then permitted to purchase full or extended rights to access the content ([0226]), which meets the limitation of enabling unobservable communication between an updater and the user-access control to control user access to the digital object when the user attempts to access the digital object, running an application using application code entirely contained within the hardware element. The full or extended rights purchased are provided by the service provider content owner to the end user, using a secure channel, where the rights object stored on the smart card is updated (Abstract & [0203] & [0226] & Figure 19B), which meets the limitation of obtaining local access to the digital object to remotely control the digital object via the updater to temporarily override access control restrictions of at least one of the plurality of NV-RAM segments on the hardware element to enable remote modification of data stored in the hardware element, temporarily overriding access control restrictions of all of the plurality of NV-RAM segments on the hardware element, temporarily overriding access control restrictions of only one of the plurality of NV-RAM segments on the hardware element. The smart card contains a user area for storage of end user data ([0075]), which meets the limitation of storing user-related information on a third part of the hardware for user application data, user application settings, and user access controls that can be controlled by the end user.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains.  Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.

The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1.	Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2.	Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3.	Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4.	Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.

Claims 1, 3-13, 15-24, 26, 28, 29, 32, 33 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Qawami, U.S. Publication No. 2007/0056042, in view of Rohrbach, U.S. Patent No. 5,898,783. Referring to claims 1, 18, 19, 29, 32, Qawami discloses a content distribution system wherein content is distributed to end users via smart cards ([0006]-[0007]), which meets the limitation of the digital object is application software or digital media. The content is stored along with a rights object that governs how/when the content can be accessed ([0009]). The rights can dictate that the content can be accessed for a limited time, and the user is then permitted to purchase full or extended rights to access the content ([0226]), which meets the limitation of executing a first portion of code on the at least one digital device in communication with the secure hardware adjunct, and using the secure hardware adjunct to execute predefined digital rights verification and enforcement located on the secure hardware adjunct configured prior to distribution of the secure hardware adjunct to the end user, running an application using application code entirely contained within the secure hardware adjunct. The full or extended rights purchased are provided by the service provider content owner to the end user, using a secure channel, where the rights object stored on the smart card is updated (Abstract & [0203] & [0226] & Figure 19B), which meets the limitation of updatable by a provider of the digital object using a secure channel after distribution of the secure adjunct to the end user. The smart card contains a user area for storage of end user data ([0075]), which meets the limitation of providing an end-user managed storage data capacity on the secure hardware adjunct for user application data, user application settings, and user access controls that can be controlled by the end user. Qawami does not specify that the smart card can be remotely disabled by the service provider. Rohrbach discloses the ability to remotely disable smart cards by their service provider (Col. 2, lines 8-11), which meets the limitation of providing another storage data capacity on the secure hardware adjunct to control user access to the digital object by allowing the provider of the digital object to disable the secure hardware adjunct, enabling a remote-disabling feature of the secure hardware adjunct upon connection of the adjunct to a digital device with a network connection, wherein the remote-disable feature is controlled by the distributor of the digital object, disabling the secure hardware adjunct. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made for the smart cards of Qawami to be disabled remotely in order to discourage theft and counterfeiting as taught by Rohrbach (Col. 2, lines 8-11).
Referring to claim 3, Qawami discloses that in order to access encrypted data from the smart card, the end user is required to enter credentials that could include passwords ([0072] & [0120]), which meets the limitation of securing against unauthorized access of end-user data that is provided by the end user by requiring a password.
Referring to claim 4, Qawami discloses that the encrypted content, the access policies, and crypto engine, are stored on the smart card (Figure 2), which meets the limitation of storing the digital object, an algorithm, and digital rights verification and enforcement data on the secure hardware adjunct using a single NV-RAM segment  having a single NV-RAM technology or a plurality of different NV-RAM segments having a plurality of different NV-RAM technologies.
Referring to claim 5, Qawami discloses that multiple levels of security can be utilized within the smart card (Figure 6 & [0264]), which meets the limitation of providing access management within the secure hardware adjunct of a plurality of NV-RAM segments, wherein the access management enables different levels of access between the plurality of NV-RAM segments to provide different levels of access to different ones of the plurality of NV-RAM segments.
Referring to claim 6, Qawami discloses that the smart card includes a public storage partition (Figure 3), which meets the limitation of the access management for at least one of the plurality of NV-RAM segments provides the end user with unrestricted read-write access.
Referring to claim 7, Qawami discloses that the smart card includes a partition with read-only access ([0122]), and a hidden partition ([0093]), which meets the limitation of the access management provides the end user with read-only access to at least one NV-RAM segment of the plurality of NV-RAM segments, no access to at least one NV-RAM segment of the plurality of NV-RAM segments.
Referring to claims 8-10, Qawami discloses accessing the content in the smart card by various user devices ([0220]), which meets the limitation of enabling communication of the digital object with the secure hardware adjunct by two-way communication by a standard or non standard interface method, integration of the secure hardware adjunct functions into a larger chip set or an integrated circuit device to support functions of the digital device, or two-way communication with the secure hardware adjunct configured and policy-managed for multi-user use over an area communication protocol, enabling communication of the digital device with the secure hardware adjunct by analog of digital interfaces, the communication of the digital device with the secure hardware adjunct is supported by hardware for the decryption or presentation of media content.
Referring to claim 11, Qawami discloses that each smart card has a unique identification ([0269]), which meets the limitation of a unique identifier is associated with the secure hardware adjunct. The limitation “to enable periodic validation of the secure hardware adjunct by the digital object using an internal clock within the secure hardware adjunct and to permit the digital object to stop working if the secure adjunct is not validated” represents an intended use of the unique identifier. A recitation of the intended use of the claimed invention must result in a structural difference between the claimed invention and the prior art in order to patentably distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art.  If the prior art structure is capable of performing the intended use, then it meets the claim.
Referring to claim 12, Qawami discloses implementing digital rights management for the digital object by having processing elements and internal RAM on the secure hardware adjunct to run at least one critical code segments and critical decryption processes directly on the secure hardware adjunct to generate values to a main application (Figure 1).
Referring to claim 13, Qawami discloses storage of data on read-write partitions, read-only partitions (Figure 5), and hidden partitions ([0093]), which meets the limitation of storing digital information on the secure hardware adjunct on NV-RAM including storage of public application enablers on an unrestricted read-write access portion of NV-RAM, storage of main application code on an unrestricted read-only access portion of NV-RAM, and storage of secret application enablers on a restricted-access portion of NV-RAM that can only be read or written to by externally unobservable internal interactions.
Referring to claim 15, Qawami discloses storing user access control on the hardware adjunct (Figure 2).
Referring to claim 16, Qawami discloses that the full or extended rights purchased are provided by the service provider content owner to the end user, using a secure channel, where the rights object stored on the smart card is updated (Abstract & [0203] & [0226] & Figure 19B), which meets the limitation of obtaining local access to the digital object to remotely control the digital object by providing an update control mechanism to temporarily override access control restrictions of at least one of the plurality of NV-RAM segments on the secure hardware adjunct to enable remote modification of data stored in the secure digital adjunct.
Referring to claim 17, Qawami discloses the digital device is a computer, PDA, a cell phone, or a gaming device (Figure 18).
Referring to claim 20, Qawami discloses that access is obtained over a secure channel ([0203]).
Referring to claim 21, Qawami discloses at least one of the plurality of NV-RAM segments is non-accessible to the end user or invisible to the end user ([0093]).
Referring to claims 22-24, Qawami discloses a content distribution system wherein content is distributed to end users via smart cards ([0006]-[0007]). The content is stored along with a rights object that governs how/when the content can be accessed ([0009]), which meets the limitation of configuring the digital object on a secure hardware adjunct to permit digital rights verification and enforcement of the digital object by a provider of the digital object irrespective of a user of the secure hardware adjunct. The rights can dictate that the content can be accessed for a limited time, and the user is then permitted to purchase full or extended rights to access the content ([0226]), which meets the limitation of automatically enabling communication between the secure hardware adjunct and the digital device when a user attempts to access the digital object, the predefined digital rights verification and enforcement located on the secure hardware adjunct control access to the digital object and is capable of blocking access to the digital object of the end user, running an application using application code entirely contained within the secure hardware adjunct. The full or extended rights purchased are provided by the service provider content owner to the end user, using a secure channel, where the rights object stored on the smart card is updated (Abstract & [0203] & [0226] & Figure 19B), which meets the limitation of controlling the digital device and user access to the digital object at a remote location by the provider of the digital object. The smart card contains a user area for storage of end user data ([0075]), which meets the limitation of providing access management having end-user access to a fourth one of the plurality of NV-RAM segments that is an end-user managed storage data capacity on the secure hardware adjunct for user application data, user application settings, and user access controls that can be controlled by the end user. Qawami discloses storage of data on read-write partitions, read-only partitions (Figure 5), which meets the limitation of unrestricted read only access to a second one of the plurality of NV-RAM segments, unrestricted read write access to a third one of the plurality of NV-RAM segments, the access management having unrestricted read only access to a second one of the plurality of NV-RAM segments is storage data capacity on the secure hardware adjunct for main application code. Qawami does not specify that the smart card can be remotely disabled by the service provider. Rohrbach discloses the ability to remotely disable smart cards by their service provider ( 2, lines 8-11), which meets the limitation of providing access management having restricted access to a first one of a plurality of NV-RAM segments the access management having restricted access to a first one of a plurality of NV-RAM segments is a storage data capacity on the secure hardware adjunct to control user access to the digital object by allowing the provider of the digital object to disable the secure hardware adjunct, controlling the digital device and user access to the digital object at a remote location to permit disabling of the secure hardware adjunct. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made for the smart cards of Qawami to be disabled remotely in order to discourage theft and counterfeiting as taught by Rohrbach ( 2, lines 8-11).
Referring to claim 26, Qawami discloses that the content can be video game software ([0006]), which meets the limitation of the digital object is application software distributed by the distributor via the secure hardware adjunct and the secure hardware adjunct allows the user to save information related to the application software on the secure hardware adjunct to permit use of the application software on different digital devices while maintaining application software settings of the user.
Referring to claim 28, the claim limitations do not serve to limit the claims because the limitations do not set forth any method steps that differentiate the claims from the prior art. MPEP 2112.02 states that a prior art device anticipates a claimed process if the device carries out the process during normal operation. 
Claim 14 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Qawami, U.S. Publication No. 2007/0056042, in view of Rohrbach, U.S. Patent No. 5,898,783, and further in view of Spurgat, U.S. Publication No. 2002/0173273. Referring to claim 14, Qawami does not disclose that the smart card includes a digital to analog converter. Spurgat discloses a portable device that includes a digital to analog converter (Figure 10), which meets the limitation of outputting from the secure hardware adjunct in an analog format by processing digital material through a digital to analog converter on the hardware adjunct. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made for the smart card of Mathers to include a digital to analog converter in order to provide a means of storing and outputting audio data files using the smart card as taught by Spurgat ([0070]).
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action.  Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL.  See MPEP § 706.07(a).  Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).  
A shortened statutory period for reply to this final action is set to expire THREE MONTHS from the mailing date of this action.  In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action.  In no event, however, will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the date of this final action.
